newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: San Miguel wins vote on Coca-Cola deal.
newsitem.headline: San Miguel wins vote on Coca-Cola deal.

text.p: Philippine food and beverage giant San Miguel Corp on Tuesday won shareholder approval for a controversial plan to merge its lucrative Coca-Cola bottling company with Australia's Coca-Cola Amatil.

It wants to swap shares in Coca-Cola Bottlers Philippines Inc, the world's sixth largest producer of the soft drink, with Amatil in what some analysts worry would leave San Miguel without one of its main sources of profit.
Its share price has slumped some 16 percent since the announcement early this month on fears that San Miguel was losing one of its cash cows, share traders said.
The proposed merger has caused such a stir in the Philippines that the shareholders meeting was televised live for the first time on state television.
The vote in favour of the deal came despite last minute opposition by local businessman Eduardo Cojuangco.
However, the former associate of late President Ferdinand Marcos was unable to vote himself because his shares have been frozen by the government which now controls San Miguel.
San Miguel wants to merge its 70 percent-owned subsidiary in exchange for a 25 percent stake in the Australian firm as part of its strategy to become more international.
Even the government, which backed the deal, had reservations about whether San Miguel was getting enough in return.

"We want a fair valuation that will increase representation in the board of Amatil from three board seats," said Magtanggol Gunigundo, chairman of the Presidential Commission on Good Government (PCGG), which holds nearly half the San Miguel shares.
But a number of other analysts had positive words for the merger after Amatil shares soared on the Australian stock market.
"The issue already appreciated by 20 percent. Where can you get 20 percent growth in two weeks," said ING Barings chief strategist Alexander Pomento.
San Miguel chairman Andres Soriano III told stockholders earlier the value of Amatil shares aquired by San Miguel had increased by nearly $400 million since the announcement.

Renato Valencia, a government representative in the San Miguel board, said "This is an excellent deal. We bought it at A$11.40 (per share). The price has gone up to A$14. After making U.S.$400 million, what more do they want?"
